body:
Electricity and the movement of charge

Electricity is a convenient form of energy used for lighting, heating, operating machines and running household appliances. To understand these applications, we must first distinguish electric charge, electric current and electric potential difference.

Electric charge is a property of matter. There are 2 kinds of electric charge: positive and negative. Like charges repel each other, while unlike charges attract each other. Electrons carry negative charge. In metallic conductors such as copper, some electrons can move through the material and carry electric current.

Electric current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a cross-section of a conductor.

\(I=\frac{Q}{t}\)

Here, \(I\) is current, \(Q\) is charge and \(t\) is time.

The SI unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C). The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A). A current of 1 A means that 1 C of charge passes through a cross-section in 1 second.

Thus, \(1\ \mathrm{A}=1\ \mathrm{C/s}\). A milliampere is one-thousandth of an ampere: \(1\ \mathrm{mA}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A}\).

Conventional current and electron flow

Before electrons were discovered, scientists established the convention that electric current flows in the direction in which positive charge would move. This convention is still used in circuit diagrams.

In the external circuit of a cell, conventional current flows from the positive terminal towards the negative terminal. Electrons in the metallic wires drift in the opposite direction, from the negative terminal towards the positive terminal.

Conventional current direction and electron drift direction are opposite in metallic conductors. The conventional direction is used in Ohm's law diagrams and the magnetic-field direction rules studied later.

How an electric circuit works

An electric circuit is a conducting path through which electric current can flow. A simple torch circuit contains an electric cell, connecting wires, a switch and a bulb. The cell maintains a potential difference between its terminals, supplying energy that moves charges through the circuit.

When the switch is closed, the circuit provides a complete conducting path and current can flow. When the switch is open, the path is broken and the bulb does not glow. A fused incandescent bulb also interrupts the current through its filament because the filament has broken.

Conductors and insulators

Materials that allow electric current to pass easily are called good conductors. Copper and aluminium are familiar examples. Materials such as dry rubber, plastic and glass are poor conductors or insulators under ordinary conditions.

Insulating materials are important because they help prevent unwanted contact with conducting parts. The metal core of a household wire carries current, while its insulating covering helps protect users.

Water containing dissolved salts can conduct electricity. Therefore, wet hands and wet surroundings increase the danger of electric shock. Ordinary household mains electricity must never be used for experiments.

Electric cells and batteries

An electric cell converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy. It has a positive terminal and a negative terminal. When 2 or more cells are connected together, the combination is called a battery. In a simple series battery, the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next.

A cell can maintain a potential difference across its terminals even when the external circuit is open. However, a steady current through a connected appliance requires a complete conducting path.

Current and charge

If a bulb draws a current of 0.5 A for 10 minutes, the time is 600 seconds. The charge that passes through it is:

\(Q=It=0.5\times600=300\ \mathrm{C}\).

Prelims focus

  • Current is charge flowing per unit time: \(I=Q/t\).
  • 1 A is equivalent to 1 C of charge per second.
  • Conventional current and electron drift have opposite directions in metallic wires.
  • A closed circuit provides a complete conducting path; an open circuit breaks that path.
  • Copper and aluminium are good electrical conductors; dry rubber and plastic are insulators.
  • Trap: A cell may have a potential difference across its terminals even when no current flows through an external circuit.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, “Electricity and Circuits,” printed pp. 116–123; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 14, “Chemical Effects of Electric Current,” printed pp. 172–176; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 171–172.]

title: Electric Charge, Electric Current and Closed Circuits

body:
Why electric current flows

Electric charges do not maintain a steady current through an ordinary metallic wire without an energy source. An electric cell or battery creates an electric potential difference between its terminals. When a conducting circuit is completed, this potential difference drives current through the connected components.

Potential difference between 2 points is the work done per unit charge in transferring charge between those points.

\(V=\frac{W}{Q}\)

Here, \(V\) is potential difference, \(W\) is work done and \(Q\) is charge.

The SI unit of potential difference is the volt (V). A potential difference of 1 V corresponds to 1 joule of work per coulomb of charge.

\(1\ \mathrm{V}=1\ \mathrm{J/C}\)

For example, transferring a charge of 2 C through a potential difference of 12 V involves an energy transfer of \(W=VQ=12\times2=24\ \mathrm{J}\).

Measuring current and potential difference

An ammeter measures electric current. It is connected in series with the component whose current is to be measured, so that the same current passes through the ammeter and that component.

A voltmeter measures potential difference between 2 points. It is connected in parallel across the component or the points under consideration.

In the ideal circuit model, an ammeter has zero resistance and a voltmeter has infinite resistance. This explains their connections: the ammeter should not appreciably obstruct the current, while the voltmeter should draw very little current from the component being measured.

Ammeter: series. Voltmeter: parallel. Interchanging these connections is not merely a measurement error; connecting an ordinary ammeter directly across a power source may create a dangerous low-resistance path.

Ohm's law

In 1827, the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm established a fundamental relationship between potential difference and current in a metallic conductor.

According to Ohm's law, the current through a given metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant.

\(V\propto I\)

Therefore, \(\frac{V}{I}=R\), or:

\(V=IR\)

The constant \(R\) is the electrical resistance of the conductor. It represents opposition to the flow of electric current. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω).

\(1\ \Omega=1\ \mathrm{V/A}\)

If a resistor has a resistance of 6 Ω and a potential difference of 12 V is applied across it, the current is \(I=V/R=12/6=2\ \mathrm{A}\), assuming the resistance remains constant.

Understanding the voltage-current graph

For a conductor obeying Ohm's law at constant temperature, a graph of potential difference \(V\) on the vertical axis against current \(I\) on the horizontal axis is a straight line passing through the origin. Its slope is \(V/I=R\).

When current is instead plotted on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis, the slope is \(I/V=1/R\). The physical relationship is unchanged, but the numerical interpretation of the graph's slope is different.

When Ohm's law must not be applied blindly

Ohm's law describes an ohmic conductor under fixed physical conditions. Not every electrical component has a constant resistance. For example, the temperature of an incandescent bulb's filament rises significantly while it operates. Its resistance changes with temperature, so its voltage-current relationship is not necessarily a straight line over a wide range.

Even for a metal wire, increasing the applied voltage may heat the wire enough to change its resistance. The constant-temperature qualification is therefore essential.

Prelims focus

  • Potential difference is work done per unit charge: \(V=W/Q\).
  • 1 volt equals 1 joule per coulomb.
  • Ammeter measures current and is connected in series.
  • Voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel.
  • Ohm's law is \(V=IR\), provided the conductor's physical conditions, especially temperature, remain constant.
  • Trap: The slope of a \(V\)-against-\(I\) graph is resistance; the slope of an \(I\)-against-\(V\) graph is its reciprocal.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 171–176, sections 11.1–11.4.]

title: Potential Difference, Ohm's Law and Electrical Measurement

body:
Resistance of a conductor

Electrical resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to electric current. Two wires connected to the same potential difference need not carry equal currents. Their resistances depend on their dimensions, materials and temperatures.

For a uniform metallic conductor at a fixed temperature, resistance depends on 3 principal factors: length, cross-sectional area and material.

Effect of length

Resistance is directly proportional to the length of a uniform wire when the material and cross-sectional area remain unchanged.

\(R\propto l\)

Therefore, if a wire's length is doubled without changing its material or thickness, its resistance doubles.

Effect of cross-sectional area

Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section when the material and length remain unchanged.

\(R\propto\frac{1}{A}\)

A thick wire offers less resistance than a thin wire of the same material and length. If the cross-sectional area becomes twice as large, resistance becomes half as much.

For a circular wire, cross-sectional area depends on the square of its radius: \(A=\pi r^2\). Consequently, doubling the diameter or radius makes the area 4 times as large and reduces resistance to one-fourth of its original value, provided the other conditions remain unchanged.

Electrical resistivity

Different materials conduct electricity differently. This material dependence is expressed through electrical resistivity, represented by the Greek letter \(\rho\) (rho).

Combining the length and area relationships gives:

\(R=\rho\frac{l}{A}\)

Equivalently, \(\rho=\frac{RA}{l}\).

The SI unit of resistivity is ohm-metre (Ω m). A material with low resistivity is generally a good electrical conductor, while a material with very high resistivity acts as an insulator under ordinary conditions.

Resistance and resistivity are not the same property. Resistance depends on both the material and the dimensions of a particular conductor. Resistivity characterises the material at a specified temperature and does not change merely because a wire of that material is made longer or thicker.

Influence of temperature

Both resistance and resistivity can change with temperature. For ordinary metallic conductors, resistance generally increases when temperature rises. This is why Ohm's law requires the temperature to remain constant when resistance is treated as fixed.

Not all materials show the same temperature behaviour. The metallic-conductor rule should not be applied indiscriminately to every substance.

Why different materials are used in electrical devices

MaterialRelevant propertyTypical application
CopperLow resistivity; good conductorElectrical wires and connections
AluminiumLow resistivity; relatively lightElectrical conductors
NichromeRelatively high resistivity; tolerates high operating temperaturesHeating elements
TungstenVery high melting pointIncandescent bulb filaments
Rubber and plasticHigh resistance under ordinary conditionsElectrical insulation

Copper and aluminium are suitable for carrying current with comparatively little heating loss because of their low resistivity. Heating devices intentionally use materials such as nichrome, which can become hot without being readily damaged at their normal operating temperatures.

In an incandescent lamp, the tungsten filament is heated sufficiently to emit visible light. Its high melting point enables it to withstand the very high temperature required.

Applying the relation

Suppose a uniform wire has a resistance of 8 Ω. A second wire of the same material and temperature is half as long and has twice the cross-sectional area.

Its resistance is:

\(R_2=8\times\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{1}{2}=2\ \Omega\).

Both dimensional changes reduce the resistance, so their effects must be multiplied.

Prelims focus

  • Resistance of a uniform wire is \(R=\rho l/A\).
  • Resistance increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area.
  • For the same material and length, doubling wire diameter reduces resistance to one-fourth.
  • Resistivity is a material property with SI unit Ω m.
  • Copper and aluminium are good conductors; nichrome is commonly used in heating elements.
  • Trap: Doubling a wire's diameter does not merely halve its resistance; the area increases 4 times.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 175–180, sections 11.4–11.5.]

title: Resistance, Resistivity and the Choice of Conducting Materials

body:
Why resistors are combined

Many electrical circuits contain more than 1 resistor or appliance. The way these components are connected determines how current and potential difference are distributed. The 2 basic arrangements are series and parallel connections.

Resistors connected in series

In a series connection, components are joined end to end so that the current passes through them along a single path. There is no branching between the components.

Consequently, the same current flows through every resistor. The total potential difference equals the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors.

For 3 resistors:

\(I=I_1=I_2=I_3\)

\(V=V_1+V_2+V_3\)

The equivalent resistance is:

\(R_s=R_1+R_2+R_3\)

The equivalent resistance of positive resistors in series is greater than any one of those resistances.

Example: 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series

Connect resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω to an ideal 6 V battery in series. Their equivalent resistance is \(R_s=2+4=6\ \Omega\).

Therefore, the current is \(I=6/6=1\ \mathrm{A}\). The potential difference across the 2 Ω resistor is \(V_1=1\times2=2\ \mathrm{V}\), while that across the 4 Ω resistor is \(V_2=1\times4=4\ \mathrm{V}\).

The individual voltage drops add to 6 V, which equals the battery voltage.

Resistors connected in parallel

In a parallel connection, each resistor is connected between the same 2 points. Electric current has more than 1 conducting path.

Therefore, the potential difference across each parallel branch is the same. The total current entering the combination is the sum of the currents through its branches.

\(V=V_1=V_2=V_3\)

\(I=I_1+I_2+I_3\)

The equivalent resistance is obtained from:

\(\frac{1}{R_p}=\frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2}+\frac{1}{R_3}\)

For 2 resistors, this becomes:

\(R_p=\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2}\)

The equivalent resistance of positive resistors connected in parallel is less than the smallest individual resistance. Adding another parallel path allows more total current to flow at the same applied voltage.

Example: 2 Ω and 4 Ω in parallel

When the same resistors are connected in parallel across 6 V, each resistor receives 6 V. The currents are \(I_1=6/2=3\ \mathrm{A}\) and \(I_2=6/4=1.5\ \mathrm{A}\).

The total current is \(3+1.5=4.5\ \mathrm{A}\). The equivalent resistance is:

\(R_p=\frac{6}{4.5}=\frac{4}{3}\ \Omega\).

Comparing the arrangements

FeatureSeries connectionParallel connection
CurrentSame through every resistorDivides among branches
Potential differenceDivided among resistorsSame across every branch
Equivalent resistanceSum of resistancesLess than the smallest branch resistance
Failure of one branch or componentA break interrupts the entire single pathOther intact branches may continue working
Household useNot suitable for independent appliance connectionsUsed for independent appliance connections

Why household appliances are connected in parallel

A fan, lamp and refrigerator need to operate independently. When appliances are connected in parallel, each receives the supply potential difference and can be controlled through its own switch. Switching off one appliance does not normally interrupt the supply to the others.

In a series arrangement, the supply voltage would be divided among the appliances, and an open circuit in one component would stop current through every component. This makes series connection unsuitable for ordinary independent household loads.

Do not confuse the total current from the source with the current through one parallel branch. The source supplies the sum of all branch currents, while each branch current depends on its own resistance and the common voltage.

Prelims focus

  • Series: current is the same through all resistors.
  • Series: \(R_s=R_1+R_2+R_3\).
  • Parallel: potential difference is the same across all branches.
  • Parallel: \(1/R_p=1/R_1+1/R_2+1/R_3\).
  • Household appliances are connected in parallel for independent operation.
  • Trap: Adding a resistor in parallel reduces equivalent resistance; adding one in series increases it.

[NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 11, “Electricity,” printed pp. 181–188, section 11.6 and its subsections on series and parallel resistors.]
